catalogue_metadata.scope_notes: Extracted from a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) codebase. Evidence is primarily static: class/symbol inventory, directory structure, workflows, and documented templates. Deep runtime behaviour (e.g. exact FlowRunner step logic, prompt content in skill markdown) was not available for direct inspection.
analysis_limits: No full source for runner.py / steps; FlowRunner pipeline inferred from symbol and directory evidence.
Skill markdown bodies and prompt text not inspected in detail; skill behaviour inferred from eval models and skill names.
Workflow YAML contents not available, only paths; CI-level agentic loops inferred.
LLM client interface contract (method signatures) not directly verified beyond class names.

system_map.overview: This repository implements a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) that orchestrates LLM-backed agents to create, validate, and evolve architecture artifacts under persistent governance. A central FlowRunner pipelines multi-step execution with a shared context, while a governance action engine restricts legal state transitions, a compliance engine validates outputs against rules, and skills with assertion-based evaluation suites make agent capabilities measurable.

agents.name: CAS FlowRunner
agents.role: Central orchestrator that executes multi-step agent pipelines and passes a shared context between steps.

agents.name: Skills Agents
agents.role: Perform domain-specific architecture tasks (add/modify feature, refactor module, generate diagrams, sync governance reviews, refactor knowledge links) via reusable skills.

agents.name: Verifier Subagent
agents.role: Reviews and verifies agent outputs before they are accepted, acting as a separate check on work produced by other agents.

orchestration.description: Central pipeline orchestration (FlowRunner) is combined with distributed, governance-enforced decision points (GovernanceActionEngine, ComplianceEngine) and skill-based autonomous subtasks. Human/system verification is delegated to a distinct verifier subagent.

patterns.name: Provider-Agnostic LLM Client with Mock Fallback

tool_protocols.notes: LLM calls are mediated by a bespoke client, not an MCP/tool-calling protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Single abstraction allows swapping vendors and enables deterministic mock-based testing.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: A thin client keeps agent flows decoupled from a specific vendor, preferring simplicity over deep vendor features.

patterns.summary: All LLM interactions are routed through a single client interface, with a parallel mock implementation for deterministic testing of agent flows.
patterns.intent: Decouple agent logic from any particular LLM vendor and make agent behaviour testable in CI without real calls.
patterns.context: The repository bundles litellm and defines a LiteLLMClient plus a MockLLMClient in the same package.
forces: Vendor drift when LLM providers change
Need for deterministic regression tests of LLM-dependent flows
Portability of the CAS runner to different environments
patterns.solution: Wrap litellm behind a dedicated client class; provide a mock client implementing the same contract and use it in test/CI contexts. The FlowRunner and steps depend on the client contract, not on a concrete provider.
implementation_signals: class LiteLLMClient defined in src/cas_runner/llm/
class MockLLMClient in the same module
litellm declared as the sole LLM dependency in pyproject.toml

evidence.note: litellm and pydantic are the core agent-facing dependencies.

benefits: Centralised place to add retries, rate limiting, and observability
costs: Potential loss of provider-specific advanced features
Mock behaviour can drift from real LLM behaviour
failure_modes: Mock diverges from real provider causing CI green but production regression
Missing interface methods when providers add new capabilities

patterns.reuse_notes: Reusable in any agent project that wants vendor-neutral LLM access and deterministic evaluation of agent workflows.

patterns.name: Sequential Pipeline Execution with Shared Mutable Context

tool_protocols.notes: Execution is driven by an explicit FlowRunner rather than emergent tool orchestration.

optimisation_targets.notes: Sequential steps with shared context favour predictability over parallelism.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: An explicit step pipeline is easier to control and audit than free-form autonomous execution.

patterns.summary: A central FlowRunner executes multi-step agent pipelines by passing a single mutable context object forward from step to step.
patterns.intent: Provide a deterministic sequential execution model for multi-step agent workflows where each step consumes and enriches a shared context.
patterns.context: src/cas_runner/runner.py exposes a FlowRunner class, strongly suggesting a step-based orchestration layer. CAS workflows (build, steering, validation, sync) are invoked as discrete stages.
forces: Need for ordered, auditable agent steps
Steps must share data without tight coupling
Trade-off between pipeline clarity and parallel execution speed
patterns.solution: Define a pipeline runner that iterates over registered steps, mutates a shared execution context, and passes it to the next step. Steps read only what they need from the context and write their outputs back to it.
implementation_signals: class FlowRunner declared in src/cas_runner/runner.py
Directory layout with governance/, llm/, dashboard/ suggesting a step-oriented package
Workflows named cas-build-*, cas-continuous-* that map to distinct pipeline stages

evidence.note: Orchestration entry point for multi-step execution.
Illustrates a governed step in the broader pipeline.

benefits: Easy to add logging/tracing around each step
costs: Sequential bottleneck on long pipelines
Mutable context risks hidden coupling between steps
failure_modes: Context grows unbounded across long pipelines
A step failing halfway leaves context in a partial state

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse the mutable-context pipeline pattern in any workflow that needs ordered, auditable agent steps (e.g. ETL-like agent flows).

patterns.name: Governance-Enforced State Transitions

tool_protocols.notes: Autonomy is constrained by an explicit transition registry rather than a tool protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Limiting legal transitions prevents agents from making illegal governance moves.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents have autonomy within a curated set of legal transitions.

patterns.summary: Legal transitions between governance states are whitelisted in a registry, so agents can only move artifacts through approved state changes.
patterns.intent: Prevent autonomous agents from performing unexpected or harmful governance state changes.
patterns.context: GovernanceActionEngine uses a TransitionRegistry to decide which transitions are permitted, and a GovernanceActionService exposes this ability to the wider CAS.
forces: Agents need autonomy to make progress
Governance requires strict control over lifecycle states
Transitions must remain auditable and reversible
patterns.solution: Maintain an explicit registry of allowed (from-state, to-state) pairs. The GovernanceActionEngine checks any requested transition against this registry before applying it, and records the action via GovernanceAction.
implementation_signals: class TransitionRegistry in governance_action_engine.py
class GovernanceActionEngine with transition-checking responsibilities
GovernanceAction model records each performed action

evidence.note: Registry of legal transitions and the engine enforcing them.
Service layer exposing governed transitions to agents.

benefits: Clear audit trail of state changes
Easy to reason about which paths are legal
costs: Updating the registry when new states are introduced
May block legitimate progress if registry is incomplete
failure_modes: Registry drift when new states are added but transitions are forgotten
Over-restrictive registry causing agent loops

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse for any agentic system that must restrict state machine transitions (e.g. document lifecycle, approval workflows).

patterns.name: Post-hoc Compliance Validation Gate

tool_protocols.notes: Validation is a separate evaluation step, not an interactive tool call.

optimisation_targets.notes: Post-hoc validation catches rule violations before artifacts become canonical.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents act freely but their outputs are checked against rules afterwards.

patterns.summary: Agent-produced artifacts are validated after the fact by a ComplianceEngine that emits structured findings and metrics.
patterns.intent: Catch rule violations in generated artifacts early and feed the results into governance health decisions.
patterns.context: ComplianceEngine produces ComplianceFinding objects that feed GovernanceHealth and GovernanceRisks; used in the continuous architecture workflow.
forces: Agent outputs can be large and free-form
Rules are complex and evolving
Feedback must be actionable and traceable
patterns.solution: Run a dedicated compliance step after generation. The engine evaluates artifacts against defined rules, returns structured ComplianceFinding and ComplianceMetrics, and the health model aggregates them into overall governance health.
implementation_signals: class ComplianceEngine in compliance_engine.py
ComplianceFinding and ComplianceMetrics models in governance/models.py
HealthStatus/calculate_health in dashboard/health_model.py consuming compliance output

evidence.note: Aggregates compliance results into health status.

benefits: Metrics feed health dashboards for steering
costs: Compliance rules must be maintained and kept in sync
Extra validation step adds latency to the pipeline
failure_modes: Incomplete rule set causes false compliance
Validation may be bypassed if workflow ordering is wrong

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any agent pipeline where generated content must be validated against organisational or regulatory rules.

patterns.name: Governance Block Injection into Agent Configuration

tool_protocols.notes: Governance is injected into agent runtime config (CLAUDE.md/settings), not via a protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Ensures every agent session sees current governance without manual copying.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents stay autonomous but are bound to injected governance blocks.

patterns.summary: Governance blocks are merged into agent runtime configuration files (CLAUDE.md, settings) so that every agent session automatically carries the latest rules.
patterns.intent: Keep agent-facing governance up to date without manual edits and enforce consistency across agent tools.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py includes merge_cas_governance_block and merge_claude_settings, and governance/agentic_merger.py provides an AgenticMerger to apply the same pattern programmatically.
forces: Governance rules change frequently
Multiple agent tools (.claude, .agents) need identical rules
Manual syncing is error-prone
patterns.solution: During bootstrap or on-demand, merge the CAS governance block into the relevant agent configuration files. AgenticMerger performs the merge in a deterministic way, and symlink/copy helpers keep skill and rule files consistent.
implementation_signals: merge_cas_governance_block and merge_claude_settings functions in bootstrap.py
class AgenticMerger in governance/agentic_merger.py
bootstrap() and init_workspace() call these merge functions

evidence.note: Entry points that inject governance into agent config.

benefits: Agents see latest rules at session start
costs: Merge logic must handle concurrent edits
Bootstrap must re-run after governance changes
failure_modes: Merge overwrites user customisations
Injection misses a newly added agent tool

patterns.reuse_notes: Reusable for any project that wants to auto-propagate policy/rule files into agent configuration directories.

patterns.name: Skills with Assertion-Based Evaluation Suites

tool_protocols.notes: Skills are evaluated via code suites, not interactive tool protocols.

optimisation_targets.notes: Evaluation suites make capability quality measurable and regression-checkable.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Skills are autonomous but must pass assertion suites before release.

patterns.summary: Agent capabilities are packaged as skills that ship with assertion-based evaluation suites, executed automatically in CI to catch regressions.
patterns.intent: Make agent skill quality measurable and automatically verifiable so broken capabilities are caught before use.
patterns.context: skills/models.py defines SkillAssertions, SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalResult; .github/workflows/cas-skill-evals.yml runs the evals. Skill directories (adding features, refactoring modules, generating drawio, syncing governance reviews) exist under .claude/skills and .agents/skills.
forces: Agent skills are code-like and can regress
Manual skill testing is expensive
Governance systems need evidence-backed quality gating
patterns.solution: Attach a set of assertions and eval cases to each skill. A CI workflow (cas-skill-evals) runs all suites and produces SkillEvalResult/SkillEvalReport records, which can be linked to runtime evaluations.
implementation_signals: SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalCase, SkillAssertions models in skills/models.py
cas-skill-evals workflow in .github/workflows/
Multiple skill directories under .claude/skills and .agents/skills

evidence.note: Data model for skill evaluation suites.
CI workflow that executes skill evaluation suites.
Example of a packaged skill with its own directory.

costs: Writing and maintaining assertion suites
Evals may take significant CI time
failure_modes: Assertions too weak to catch real issues
Evals tightly coupled to one environment and flaky in CI

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt in any agent framework where skills/plugins need automated quality gates and regression testing.

patterns.name: Persistent Governance Blackboard (Knowledge Base)

tool_protocols.notes: Agents coordinate via a shared file-based knowledge base, not via message passing.

optimisation_targets.notes: Shared blackboard gives persistent evidence and audit trail to agent work.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents autonomously read/write to a governed shared memory.

patterns.summary: All governance knowledge (decisions, rules, patterns, signals, narratives, project records) is stored in a persistent, file-based blackboard that agents read and write.
patterns.intent: Give agents shared, durable memory of governance and architecture evidence to avoid state loss and enable cross-session coordination.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/ organises content under global/{decisions,governance,maps,models,narratives,patterns,rules,signals} and projects/<project>/ directories, with runtime/evaluations and runtime/traces for derived state.
forces: Agent decisions must be auditable
Work spans multiple sessions/agents
Knowledge must be reusable across projects
patterns.solution: Persist all governance artifacts as structured files in the cas-knowledge tree. Agents use the global and project folders as a blackboard, and runtime folders capture ephemeral traces and evaluations. Templates in cas-knowledge/templates define the shape of each artifact.
implementation_signals: Directory structure with global/ and projects/ under cas-knowledge/
Subdirectories for decisions, rules, patterns, signals, maps, models, narratives
runtime/traces and runtime/evaluations for derived state

evidence.note: Telemetry traces stored as runtime memory.

benefits: Shared context across agents and sessions
costs: File-based store can be slow to query
Requires careful governance of file layout
failure_modes: Stale records if merges are not atomic
File conflicts when multiple agents write simultaneously

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse the blackboard layout (global vs project vs runtime) in any multi-agent system that needs shared durable memory.

patterns.name: Template-Contract Enforcement for Agent Artifacts

tool_protocols.notes: Artifact structure is enforced by markdown/json schema templates rather than a schema registry.

optimisation_targets.notes: Standardised templates reduce variance in agent-generated artifacts.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents fill in defined templates rather than designing ad-hoc outputs.

patterns.summary: All governance artifacts (ADRs, patterns, rules, signals, experiments) are generated from predefined templates that act as contracts on agent output structure.
patterns.intent: Ensure agent-produced artifacts are consistently structured and machine-parseable.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/templates contains dedicated templates for ADRs, patterns, signals, rules, experiments, learning, diagrams, and promotion decisions.
forces: Agents produce heterogeneous output
Downstream tools (portal, validation) need predictable structure
Human review is simpler with standard formats
patterns.solution: Provide a template file for each artifact type, e.g. pattern_template.md, signal_template.md, rule_template.md, and have the agent fill those templates when generating content. This makes outputs consistent and enables automated parsing.
implementation_signals: Multiple template files in cas-knowledge/templates/
Templates named after artifact types (pattern, signal, rule, learning)
Presence of architecture_work_template.md and architecture_intent_template.md for workflow control

benefits: Faster human review with standard formats
costs: Templates must be maintained when domain evolves
Over-rigid templates can constrain creative outputs
failure_modes: Agents fill placeholders incorrectly or leave them empty
Template drift when new artifact types are added without templates

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse the template contract approach for any agent system that generates structured documents at scale.

patterns.name: Evidence-Based Heuristic-to-Pattern Promotion

tool_protocols.notes: Knowledge evolution is governed by explicit promotion decision records.

optimisation_targets.notes: Avoids premature canonisation of agent-learned heuristics.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Promotion is a controlled, evidence-gated decision rather than automatic.

patterns.summary: Reusable heuristics observed in agent work are promoted to formal patterns only after an explicit decision record with evidence, rather than becoming canonical automatically.
patterns.intent: Prevent unvalidated heuristics from being treated as authoritative patterns in the knowledge base.
patterns.context: Dedicated templates exist for heuristic-to-pattern conversion and promotion decisions (heuristic-to-pattern_template.md, promotion_decision.md), and global/patterns stores the result.
forces: Agents learn new practices continuously; not all should become patterns
Patterns must be evidence-backed to be trustworthy
Promotion should be auditable
patterns.solution: Represent heuristics and patterns as distinct artifact types. Use a dedicated promotion decision template to record evidence and rationale before moving a heuristic to the global/patterns folder.
implementation_signals: cas-knowledge/templates/heuristic-to-pattern_template.md
cas-knowledge/templates/promotion_decision.md
cas-knowledge/global/patterns/ and global/rules/ directories for canonical storage

benefits: Prevents premature canonisation of unvalidated heuristics
Maintains trust in the pattern catalogue
costs: Extra ceremony may slow down knowledge capture
Requires culture of writing promotion decisions
failure_modes: Promotion decisions bypass the template
Evidence quality is low leading to weak patterns

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse in any agentic system that wants to evolve a knowledge base from observed heuristics to validated patterns.

patterns.name: Governance Health Aggregation for Steering

tool_protocols.notes: Health status is computed from compliance metrics to steer workflow decisions.

optimisation_targets.notes: Aggregated health gives a single decision signal for steering.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: A deterministic health score gives humans/agents a simple steering cue.

patterns.summary: Compliance, throughput, and risk metrics are aggregated into a HealthStatus so that steering actions are based on a single, explainable readiness signal.
patterns.intent: Give agents and humans a single, explainable readiness signal to guide when to proceed, pause, or escalate.
patterns.context: dashboard/health_model.py defines HealthStatus and calculate_health, and governance/models.py holds GovernanceHealth/GovernanceThroughput/GovernanceRisks that feed it.
forces: Many metrics can overwhelm decision-making
Steering needs a decisive summary
Health must be explainable for governance
patterns.solution: Map compliance findings and governance metrics into a small set of health statuses (with reasons). calculate_health produces the status, get_health_reasons explains it, and the CAS uses this to gate or steer workflows (e.g. portal publish, steering sync).
implementation_signals: HealthStatus enum in health_model.py
calculate_health and get_health_reasons functions
GovernanceHealth, GovernanceThroughput, and GovernanceRisks models in governance/models.py

benefits: Clear steering signals for agents and humans
costs: Aggregation can hide nuance
Health thresholds need tuning per project
failure_modes: Overly coarse health masks underlying issues
Thresholds not calibrated cause false steering actions

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse the health-aggregation pattern for any governance/ops system that needs a simple steering signal from many metrics.

patterns.name: Shared State and Resource Sync via Symlink/Copy

tool_protocols.notes: Resource sharing is implemented via symlinks/copies, not a network protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Symlink/copy sync keeps agent environments consistent across tools.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Using the filesystem as a shared resource avoids complex sync services.

patterns.summary: Shared agent resources (skills, rules, configs) are synchronised across tool directories (.claude, .agents) via symlinks or copies during bootstrap to avoid drift.
patterns.intent: Keep agent-facing resources consistent across different agent tools and workspaces without manual duplication.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py includes _create_symlink_or_copy, bootstrap, and init_workspace; the directory tree mirrors skills in both .claude/skills and .agents/skills.
forces: Multiple agent tools require the same skill files
Manual duplication is error-prone
Different platforms may need symlink vs copy
patterns.solution: During bootstrap, create symlinks or copies so that the canonical skill/rule files are visible in each tool directory (e.g. .claude and .agents). Use copies on platforms where symlinks are not supported.
implementation_signals: function _create_symlink_or_copy in bootstrap.py
identical skill directory names under .agents/skills and .claude/skills
bootstrap/init_workspace invoked to set up environment

benefits: Consistent skill availability across agent tools
costs: Symlink/copy logic can be tricky on Windows
Copies can drift if bootstrap not re-run
failure_modes: Broken symlinks in some environments
Copies go stale when canonical files change but bootstrap is not run

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse for any project using multiple agent tools that need identical skill/rule files; prefer symlinks and use copies as fallback.

anti_patterns.name: Duplicated Skill Definitions Across Agent Tools
symptoms: Same skill directories (cas-add-or-modify-feature, cas-drawio-generator, etc.) appear in both .agents/skills and .claude/skills
Skill files are physically duplicated or rely on symlink/copy that can be skipped
Two independent configuration trees (.agents and .claude) hold the same capabilities
impact: Skill behaviours can drift between agent tools, producing inconsistent agent actions
Maintenance burden doubles when updating a skill
Verification results may apply to one tool but not the other, reducing trust in governance
suggested_remediation: Use symlinks as the canonical sync mechanism, with a CI check that verifies no divergence
Centralise skill definitions in a single source-of-truth directory and generate tool-specific bindings
Add a workflow (e.g. in cas-build-validation) that fails if hashes of mirrored skill files do not match

anti_patterns.name: Governance Blocks Injected Without Clear Visibility
symptoms: mergers (merge_claude_settings, AgenticMerger) apply governance blocks to agent config without a visible diff/audit in normal flow
Governance changes propagate automatically only on bootstrap/merge runs, which humans may not see
Agents may act on rules injected after they were spawned, with no way to retroactively check which version applied

where_observed.note: Injection of governance into agent config.

impact: Agent decisions can be influenced by rules the user did not explicitly approve
Debugging becomes harder because the exact governance snapshot is not recorded per run
Potential for silent divergence between what was reviewed and what runs
suggested_remediation: Record a governance snapshot (hash/version) with each execution trace so the applied rules are auditable
Emit a visible diff when governance blocks change, and force an explicit approval step in CI
Expose a command (e.g. cas_runner CLI) that prints the current effective governance and its provenance

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Template files act as the primary prompt/artifact contract; skills ship with assertions; governance blocks are injected into agent config to constrain prompts.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Prompts are not hard-coded in the runner; they are externalised as skill templates and governance rules, increasing maintainability and consistency.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Multi-level evaluation: skill eval suites (CI), compliance engine (post-generation), and health aggregation (steering).
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Evaluation is layered so a failure at the skill level is caught before governance compliance, and health aggregation guides high-level steering.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Governance transition whitelist (TransitionRegistry) and mock-based deterministic testing constrain what agents may do and how their behaviours are verified.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Safety is achieved by explicit state-machine control and by running agent behaviour against deterministic mocks before real interactions.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Provider abstraction through LiteLLM allows swapping vendors/budgets; mock client enables zero-cost tests and local development.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: No explicit cost limits observed in code, but the abstraction is the right seam for adding rate/cost controls later.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: OpenTelemetry dependency, runtime trace storage, and dashboard health reporting give visibility into agent execution.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Tracing is partially inferred (deps + directory); actual trace emission points were not visible in the symbol inventory.

open_questions.evidence_gap: Only the class name FlowRunner was available; step definitions, context object, and order were not inspected.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Read src/cas_runner/runner.py and any src/cas_runner/steps/ modules for step registration and context handling.

open_questions.question: Are governance action transitions actually enforced at runtime, or is TransitionRegistry only used in documentation/tests?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether the governance constraint pattern is a live safeguard or a paper feature.
open_questions.evidence_gap: TransitionRegistry is named but no call sites were visible in the symbol list.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Grep for calls to GovernanceActionEngine/TransitionRegistry across src/ and workflows.

open_questions.question: What is the actual prompt structure used by skills (e.g. how are skill templates turned into LLM prompts)?

open_questions.evidence_gap: No prompt-assembly code or skill markdown bodies were in scope.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Inspect .claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md and any LLM client prompt-builder functions.

open_questions.question: How is parallel execution handled across projects (there are multiple cas-knowledge/projects)?

open_questions.evidence_gap: No concurrency primitives (threading/async/fan-out) were present in the symbol inventory.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Search for asyncio, ThreadPoolExecutor, or multiprocessing usage; check workflow concurrency settings.
